purpose: The exact set of (sealed attempt, product file) attestations, the hash of every sealed report that makes them, and an honest statement of how much of the tree they cover. Superset checks, not counts: a review demonstrated that a count-only census is bypassed by deleting one pin and adding a decoy of equal count.
report_hashes_purpose: A review found that no seal protects report.json itself and the evidence ledger carries no hash chain, so editing a pin in place was cheaper and more invisible than declaring a supersession — the honest path was the expensive one. Sealed reports never legitimately change, so pinning them costs nothing and closes that route.
coverage_purpose: Pinned files cover a small minority of the tree. That is stated rather than implied, because a gate that reads as comprehensive and is not is worse than no gate.

coverage.note: None of the top-level schemas amended in the integrity-hardening wave is itself pinned by any seal; the projection copies under src/epistemic_foundry/_canonical/ are, which is why the wave surfaced there. Authoring-schema integrity is enforced by verify_projection and the canonical-hash contract gates, not by these pins.

limitation: assertions_sha256 is the sha256 of the very list it certifies, so this file is self-certifying and detects nothing an editor cannot recompute. A review demonstrated it: a three-file edit -- rewrite a sealed report's pin, rewrite the census entry, recompute the digest -- passes every gate. This is stated rather than papered over, because there is no key material or external anchor in this repository to root the trust in. What the census does buy is that the cheap two-file edit is closed and the remaining attack must be internally consistent across three files. It raises cost; it is not tamper-proof and must never be described as such.
